name: Choosing a Vocational Training (TVET) Program
objectives: Given your own interests and what you can find out about jobs where you live, list three trades that fit you and are in demand locally, with at least one piece of job-market evidence for each, such as job ads or an employer you asked

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Finding the right trade and the right kind of program

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What TVET is and where it can lead
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name five trades or technical jobs that TVET programs prepare people for.
This lesson builds toward: Given your own interests and what you can find out about jobs where you live, you will list three trades that fit you and are in demand locally, with at least one piece of job-market evidence for each, such as job ads or an employer you asked.
TVET stands for Technical and Vocational Education and Training. UNESCO describes it as education, training and skills development for a wide range of jobs and ways of earning a living. In plain words: TVET teaches you to do a job with your hands, tools and know-how.
TVET happens in many places: technical and vocational colleges, polytechnics, training centres, apprenticeships with an employer or master craftsperson, and some secondary schools. Names differ: a polytechnic in Ghana or Nigeria, a TVET college in Kenya, a TESDA-registered training centre in the Philippines, a CONALEP school in Mexico, a SENA centre in Colombia, a community college in the US.
Trades include building (electrician, plumber, mason, carpenter, welder), machines and vehicles (motor mechanic, motorcycle repair, refrigeration and air conditioning), services (hairdressing, beauty, tailoring, catering and cooking, hotel work), care (nursing assistant, caregiver), farming and food processing, and technology (computer repair, networking, solar installation, phone repair).
A good TVET program can lead to a job, an apprenticeship, your own small business, or further study. A poor one leads nowhere, so the rest of this course is about choosing well.
Words to know:
- TVET: Technical and Vocational Education and Training: learning a job skill through practice, not only books.
- Trade: a skilled job you learn by training and practice, such as plumbing or tailoring.
- Polytechnic: a college that teaches technical and practical subjects, often up to diploma level.
Official sources:
- UNESCO-UNEVOC TVETipedia: Technical and vocational education and training
Try it now: On paper, write the five trades from this lesson that interest you most. Next to each, write one person you know who does that work or something close to it.
You can now say what TVET is, where it is taught, and name five trades it can lead to.

check.q: What does a TVET program mainly teach?
options: Only theory from books
How to pass any university exam
A job skill through practice with tools
How to get a visa
check.why: TVET is training for a job or trade, with hands-on practice.

check.q: Which of these is a TVET path?
options: A two-year electrical installation course at a technical college
A lottery ticket
A social media page about fashion
A loan from a moneylender
check.why: A technical college course in a trade is a TVET program.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Choosing a trade that fits you and the local jobs
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List three trades that fit your interests and show evidence that each is in demand where you live.
This lesson builds toward: Given your own interests and what you can find out about jobs where you live, you will list three trades that fit you and are in demand locally, with at least one piece of job-market evidence for each, such as job ads or an employer you asked.
Start with you. Do you like working indoors or outdoors? With people, machines, food, fabric or computers? Are you good with numbers, careful with details, strong, patient? Do you want a job with a company or your own business?
Then look at the jobs. A trade you love is hard to live from if nobody near you is hiring or buying. Find evidence: count job ads for the trade on job boards, in newspapers and on notice boards; ask two or three employers or business owners what skills they cannot find; ask people working in the trade how easy it was to find work and customers.
Some governments publish labour market information, such as lists of skills in demand. Look for it on your labour ministry's website. Be careful with lists you see in advertisements or social media posts: a school selling a course will always say its trade is in demand.
Pick three trades that fit you and have some evidence of demand. You will compare programs for them in the next lessons.
Step by step:
- Write what you like and what you are good at.
- List trades that match.
- For each, find evidence of jobs: ads, employers, people in the trade.
- Keep the three trades with the best fit and the best evidence.
Words to know:
- Demand: how many employers or customers want a skill.
- Labour market information: facts about jobs: which are growing, what they pay and what skills they need.
Try it now: Make a table with three rows, one per trade. Columns: why it fits me, evidence of jobs (for example "5 ads this week" or "the garage owner said he needs a trained mechanic"), and where I found it. Fill every box.
You can now choose three trades that fit you and back each one with real evidence of local demand.

check.q: Which is the best evidence that a trade is in demand where you live?
options: A school's advertisement says so
You counted many job ads and two employers said they need it
A friend online said it pays well everywhere
It is popular in another country
check.why: Job ads and employers near you are real evidence; ads from a school selling the course are not.

check.q: You love fashion design, but you found no jobs nearby. What is a sensible next step?
options: Give up on any training
Enrol in the first course you see
Look for customers and related trades, like tailoring, and check demand for those
Pay an agent to find you a job abroad
check.why: Related trades with local demand can use the same interest and give you a way to earn.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Types of programs and the credential you earn
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare program types by length, entry requirements, cost and the credential you earn.
This lesson builds toward: Given two or more training options, you will compare programs by type, length, entry requirements, full cost and the credential earned, in a written table with no empty boxes.
TVET comes in several kinds. Short courses last days to a few months and teach one skill. Certificate and diploma programs at colleges and polytechnics last longer and usually mix classroom theory with workshop practice. National certificates, such as those issued through TESDA in the Philippines, are based on national standards and an assessment. Apprenticeships put you to work with an employer or master craftsperson while you learn; in the US, Registered Apprenticeships are listed on apprenticeship.gov. Dual training splits your time between a school and a company.
In many countries, especially in West Africa, many young people learn through informal apprenticeships with a master craftsperson. These can teach real skills, but the certificate may not be recognized. Ask if you can also sit a national trade test or assessment to get a recognized credential.
Compare each option on the same five points: type of program, length, entry requirements (for example a school certificate or a minimum age), full cost, and the credential you get at the end and who issues it. A credential issued by or recognized by the national authority is worth more to employers than a certificate printed by the school alone.
Step by step:
- Write the options for one trade.
- For each one, note the type and the length.
- Note the entry requirements.
- Note the full cost (fees, tools, uniform, exam, transport).
- Note the credential and who issues or recognizes it.
Words to know:
- Credential: a certificate, diploma or licence that proves your skill.
- Apprenticeship: learning a trade by working with a skilled person or employer, often with pay.
- Assessment: a test where you show your skill, often by doing a real task.
Official sources:
- TESDA (Philippines)
- Apprenticeship.gov (US Department of Labor)
Try it now: For your top trade, find two different kinds of program (for example a college certificate and an apprenticeship). Make a table with the five points: type, length, entry requirements, full cost and credential. Write "unknown" where you still need to ask.
You can now compare training programs on type, length, entry requirements, full cost and the credential they give.

check.q: Which credential is usually worth the most to employers?
options: A certificate the school printed itself
A certificate from a social media course
A letter from a friend
A credential issued or recognized by the national TVET authority
check.why: National recognition tells employers the training met an official standard.

options: Only the first month's fee
Fees, tools, uniform, exam fees and transport
Only the price on the poster
Nothing; good programs are always free
check.why: Hidden costs like tools, exams and transport can double what you pay.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Checking the school and making your choice

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Is it accredited? Checking the official register
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check on the national TVET authority's official website that a school and its program are registered or accredited.
This lesson builds toward: Given the name of a school and a program, you will check on the national TVET authority's official register that the school and program are accredited, and write down where you checked and what it showed.
Most countries have a government body that registers or accredits TVET schools and programs. Accredited means the authority checked that the school meets its standards. A certificate from an unaccredited school may not be accepted by employers, by other schools, or for a job abroad.
Examples: in Kenya, the TVET Authority (TVETA) licenses, registers and accredits institutions and publishes a list of accredited institutions at tveta.go.ke. In Nigeria, the National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) regulates TVET institutions such as polytechnics and technical colleges. In the Philippines, TESDA lists training institutions with registered programs. In Ghana, look for the Commission for TVET (CTVET); in India, the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) and Skill India; in Morocco, the OFPPT is a large public provider; in Mexico, CONALEP is a public technical school system; in Colombia, SENA is the public training service. In Senegal, Egypt and other countries, start with the ministry in charge of vocational or technical education. In the US, check Registered Apprenticeships on apprenticeship.gov and ask your state about licensed schools.
Check the name of the school AND the program. A school can be registered while one of its courses is not. Use the official website (often ending in .gov, .go.ke, .gov.ng, .gov.ph or your country's government ending), not a link sent by the school or an agent. If you cannot find the school, call or visit the authority's office and ask.
Step by step:
- Find your country's TVET authority from the ministry of education or labour website.
- Open its official website yourself; do not use a link from the school.
- Search the register for the exact school name and branch.
- Check that your program is listed too.
- Write down the website, the date and what it showed. If it is not there, ask the authority directly.
Words to know:
- Accredited: checked and approved by an official body as meeting its standards.
- Register: an official list, here of approved schools and programs.
- Authority: the government body in charge of something, here of TVET.
Official sources:
- TVETA Kenya: accredited TVET institutions
- National Board for Technical Education (Nigeria)
- TESDA (Philippines): registered programs
- Apprenticeship.gov (US)
Try it now: Find the official TVET authority for your country. Open its website yourself and look up one school near you and the program you want. Write down the website address, today's date and what you found. If you could not find the school, write the phone number or office you will ask.
You can now find your country's TVET authority and check on its official register that a school and its program are accredited.

check.q: A school sends you a link to "prove" it is accredited. What do you do?
options: Trust the link because it looks official
Open the authority's official website yourself and search for the school
Pay the fee first and check later
Ask the school's agent if it is true
check.why: A link from the school could lead to a fake page; go to the official site yourself.

check.q: The school is on the register, but your course is not listed. What is true?
options: The course is surely fine
Only the building needs to be registered
The course may not be accredited; ask the authority before you enrol
It does not matter for employers
check.why: Schools and programs are often checked separately; check the program too.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Questions to ask, and how to spot a fake school
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Ask a school six key questions and name the warning signs of a training scam.
This lesson builds toward: Before you enrol, you will ask a school about hands-on practice, equipment, trainers, the final exam, job results and the full cost, and write down the answer to every question. Given an advertisement, message or offer about training, you will spot the warning signs of a fake school or training scam, naming at least two signs when they are present and not paying before you check.
Visit the school if you can, and ask: How many hours of hands-on practice will I have? Can I see the workshop and the equipment? Who are the trainers, and have they worked in the trade? What exam or assessment is at the end, and who gives the certificate? How many past students found work or started a business, and can I talk to one? What is the full cost, including tools, exams and uniforms, and what is the refund rule? Write down every answer.
Good schools answer clearly and let you see the workshop. Be careful if they only show a classroom, cannot name an employer who hires their graduates, or will not put fees in writing.
Warning signs of a fake school or scam: a promised or "guaranteed" job, especially abroad; pressure to pay today; fees paid to a person's phone or account instead of the school's official account with a receipt; no real address; a full certificate in a few days with no practice; asking to keep your passport or ID card. Never pay to get a job, keep your own documents, and check the school on the official register first.
If you think it is a scam, do not pay. Report it to the TVET authority or the police, and warn friends.
Step by step:
- Ask about hands-on hours, the workshop and equipment.
- Ask who the trainers are and what experience they have.
- Ask about the final exam and who issues the certificate.
- Ask about past students' jobs and the full cost and refunds.
- Write down every answer and compare with the warning signs.
Words to know:
- Refund: money paid back to you if you leave or the course is cancelled.
- Receipt: a written or printed record that you paid, with the school's name.
Try it now: Write the six questions on a page. Ask them to one school, by visit or phone, or ask someone who studied there. Write every answer. Then circle any warning sign you heard.
You can now ask a school the questions that matter, record the answers and spot the warning signs of a fake school.

check.q: Which question best tells you how much real practice you will get?
options: "Is the uniform nice?"
"Do you have a website?"
"Is the school near a bus stop?"
"How many hours will I work in the workshop with real equipment?"
check.why: Hands-on hours and real equipment are how you learn a trade.

check.q: A recruiter says: "Pay today to my phone and you get a guaranteed job abroad after the course." What is this?
options: A scam warning sign; do not pay
A normal school offer
A government scholarship
A good deal if it is cheap
check.why: Guaranteed jobs, pressure to pay now and paying to a personal phone are classic scam signs.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Comparing and deciding: your program decision plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page program decision plan with your choice, costs, funding and dates.
This lesson builds toward: Given two or more training options, you will compare programs by type, length, entry requirements, full cost and the credential earned, in a written table with no empty boxes. Using your comparison and checks, you will write a program decision plan with your choice, costs, funding and dates, that another person could follow.
Put your two best programs side by side in one table: type, length, entry requirements, full cost, credential and who issues it, accreditation (where you checked), answers to your six questions, and any warning signs. The best choice is not always the cheapest: it is the accredited program with the most practice and the best evidence that graduates find work.
Plan how you will pay. Write the full cost and when each payment is due. Look for help from official sources only: government bursaries, loans or free public training in some countries, scholarships from employers or community groups, or an apprenticeship that pays you while you learn. Check any funding offer on the official website of the agency that gives it, and never pay a fee to get a scholarship.
Write the dates: when applications open and close, what documents you need (keep the originals yourself and give copies), the start date, and the date of the final exam. Show your plan to a parent, teacher, counsellor or someone in the trade, and ask what you missed.
Step by step:
- Make a table comparing your two best programs.
- Choose one and write why.
- Write the full cost, payment dates and how you will pay.
- Write the documents, application deadline, start date and exam date.
- Show the plan to someone you trust and fix what they find.
Words to know:
- Bursary: money given to help a student pay for school, which you do not pay back.
- Deadline: the last day to do something, such as apply.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page program decision plan: your trade and why, two programs compared, where you checked accreditation, the school's answers, warning signs, your choice, how you will pay, and dates for applying, starting and the final exam. Show it to one person you trust.
You can now compare two programs and write a decision plan with your choice, costs, funding, documents and dates.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Trade fits you and local jobs The trade is chosen with no reason or no evidence of demand. Says why the trade fits and gives at least one piece of local job evidence. Gives evidence from two or more sources, such as job ads and an employer conversation. Programs compared Only one program, or the table has empty boxes. Two programs compared on type, length, entry requirements, full cost and credential. Also includes hidden costs and who issues or recognizes each credential. Accreditation checked No check, or the check used a link from the school. School and program checked on the national authority's official site, with where and when. Also contacted the authority to confirm anything unclear. Questions asked and scams screened No answers from the school recorded, or warning signs ignored. Answers to the six questions recorded and any warning signs named. Also talked to a past student or an employer about the school. Decision plan No choice, cost or dates. A clear choice with full cost, how to pay, documents and dates. Reviewed by a trusted person, with their feedback added. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Someone offers you a scholarship if you first pay a "processing fee". What do you do?
options: Pay quickly before it closes
Send a copy of your passport to hold the place
Do not pay; check the scholarship on the official agency's website
Borrow money to pay the fee
check.why: Real scholarships do not charge you to receive them; check them on the official site.

check.q: Program A is cheaper but not accredited. Program B costs more, is accredited and has a full workshop. Which is usually the better choice?
options: Program A, because it is cheaper
Neither; never train
Whichever finishes fastest
Program B, if you can find a way to pay
check.why: An accredited program with real practice is worth more to employers than a cheap unrecognized one.
